sources.entry: (Un)Reliability Budgets - Finding Balance between Innovation and Reliability

summary.name: (Un)Reliability Budgets
summary.one_liner: A 2015 USENIX ;login: article by Google SRE Mark Roth describing the "unreliability budget," a metric-based method for balancing feature velocity against service reliability.
use_cases: Deciding how often to push releases to production
Negotiating risk between product developers and SRE teams
Setting a quarterly reliability target for a service
Choosing between quick fixes and full testing after a rollback
summary.what_it_does: The article explains the structural tension between Product Development (measured on velocity) and SRE (measured on reliability) and lists recurring disputes over testing, push frequency, canary duration and size, and retry after reverted pushes. It proposes a quarterly unreliability budget, derived from an SLO set by Product Management and measured by Google's monitoring system. The budget is the allowed gap between target and actual uptime; releases pause once it is spent, except critical fixes. A hypothetical example shows 0.0002% of failures consuming 20% of a 0.001% budget. The author argues the budget makes teams self-policing and highlights that over-exceeding an SLO signals too little risk-taking.
notable: Quarterly unreliability budget derived from SLO, measured by an independent monitoring system
Worked example: 0.0002% failure against 0.001% budget equals 20% consumed
Freezes non-critical pushes once the budget is spent
Frames over-exceeding an SLO as a sign of over-provisioning or insufficient risk-taking
caveats: Describes Google's internal practice; the article gives no tooling or implementation details
Actual SLOs at Google may be more complex, involving latency and data freshness
